LIMBO: Lifelong Inference-Time Memory and Budget Optimization for LLM Agents

Siddharth Sharma1, Nilesh Prasad Pandey1, Onat Gungor2, Tajana Rosing1 Affiliation: 1University of California, San Diego, CA, USA
2West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA
{sis004, nppandey, tajana}@ucsd.edu, onat.gungor@wvu.edu
Abstract

As LLM agents become integrated into increasingly complex workflows, they must continually acquire new capabilities while retaining competence on previously learned tasks. Lifelong agents address this through experience replay, injecting past interactions into the prompt to leverage prior experience during inference. However, replay is not free: every replayed trajectory competes with retrieval, reasoning, tool use, and verification for the same limited prompt and compute budget, making effective resource allocation essential. Existing approaches allocate these resources using fixed replay policies, regardless of whether replay is beneficial for the current task. We identify this as inference-time memory allocation, a distinct problem class for lifelong agents, and introduce LIMBO: the first online framework to our knowledge that treats memory as a controllable inference-time resource and jointly optimizes memory strategy and inference budget for each incoming task. Unlike prior approaches that fix the replay policy or require model weights, teacher supervision, or offline retraining, LIMBO learns this allocation online in a single pass, explicitly balancing task performance and inference cost without modifying the underlying agent. Across three LLM backbones on LifelongAgentBench, LIMBO achieves better cost-accuracy tradeoffs than state-of-the-art memory-augmented baselines, and nearly matches all strongest such baselines at up to ∼\sim83% lower inference cost (∼\sim53% on average). LIMBO adapts its policy across models and environments without retraining, demonstrating that effective allocation can be learned online rather than manually specified.

Index Terms: 
lifelong learning, LLM agents, contextual bandit, inference-time compute, experience replay, cost-aware control

I Introduction

LLM agents are increasingly deployed in environments where they must solve a continuous stream of evolving tasks while accumulating experience over time [1, 2, 3]. Unlike conventional single-task settings, these agents can leverage accumulated experiences from previous interactions to improve future performance through mechanisms such as memory, retrieval, and tool use [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. However, these mechanisms compete for limited inference-time resources, including context length, computational budget, and latency, creating a fundamental tradeoff between leveraging accumulated experience and maintaining inference efficiency [9]. As lifelong agents encounter diverse tasks and environments, effectively allocating these resources becomes critical for preserving prior knowledge while adapting to new challenges [10].

Memory represents one of the most critical components in this resource-allocation problem, as lifelong agents must decide which past experiences to retain and retrieve under limited inference-time budgets. Among existing approaches, experience replay has become a widely adopted mechanism for leveraging historical interactions [10]. Experience replay injects past trajectories into the current task prompt, enabling agents to reuse previously acquired tool-use patterns, command templates, and action-format conventions without requiring parameter updates. However, despite its effectiveness in improving agent performance, replay introduces significant scalability challenges as agents accumulate more experience. As the task count tt increases, the replay buffer grows proportionally, resulting in an 𝒪⁡(t)\mathcal{O}(t) increase in the number of injected tokens and corresponding inference-time overhead. Moreover, the utility of individual trajectories can vary substantially depending on the current task, model, and environment. Consequently, uniform replay strategies may incur considerable context and computation costs by allocating resources to trajectories that provide limited benefit for the current task.

This cost-value mismatch is not merely a theoretical concern; it appears empirically across environments and replay strategies. Figure 1 illustrates that increasing fixed replay buffers provides diminishing performance improvements while incurring rapidly growing inference costs. Scaling fixed replay from no-replay to k=16k{=}16 on DBBench [10] with Qwen2.5 7B raises inference cost by more than 5×5\times but improves accuracy by only 2 points, with the k=8→k=16k{=}8\to k{=}16 step being effectively flat. Compression-based approaches [4, 11] reduce token overhead but tend to disrupt the structured action traces required by interactive environments. Retrieval-based strategies [12] improve memory relevance but still introduce additional selection costs and consume limited context capacity. These limitations reveal a fundamental challenge: effective lifelong agents must determine not only which experiences to replay, but also when replay provides sufficient value to justify its inference-time cost. More broadly, agents must dynamically allocate limited resources across memory, retrieval, reasoning, tool use, and verification, which all compete for the same context and computation budgets.

We address this challenge with LIMBO, a lifelong controller that adaptively allocates inference-time memory and compute resources. For each incoming task, LIMBO selects a memory strategy and compute budget using a lightweight contextual bandit based on prompt and runtime features. This formulation provides a unified online allocation framework over existing memory mechanisms, including fixed replay, prompt compression, selective replay [12, 13], and memory-augmented agents [14, 15]. Across three LLM backbones evaluated on LifelongAgentBench, LIMBO achieves comparable or superior performance to the strongest fixed replay baseline while reducing inference cost by up to ∼\sim83%. Furthermore, LIMBO learns different memory allocation policies across model and environment configurations, highlighting the importance of adaptive inference-time resource management.

II Related Work

Lifelong Learning and LLM Agent Benchmarks. Lifelong learning aims to retain knowledge across sequential tasks without forgetting [16], with classical approaches based on regularization [17] and experience replay [12]. These methods target static supervised settings; extending them to LLM agents that act and adapt across interactive environments remains largely unexplored [10], and prior replay methods carry no mechanism for adaptive inference time budget allocation. Existing agent benchmarks such as WebArena [2], AgentBench [1], and VisualWebArena [3] evaluate isolated tasks in static environments, with no protocol for sequential skill transfer. LifelongAgentBench (LAB) [10] addresses this gap with three interactive environments, explicit skill labels, a skill dependency graph, and automatic label verification, providing a clean setting in which fixed, compressed, retrieved, and gated replay can be compared under one protocol.

Agent Efficiency. Recent work on adaptive reasoning and budget-aware inference studies how much computation an LLM should spend at test time [5, 6, 7, 8, 18], and cascade methods learn budget constrained routing across models or inference paths [19]. Empirical analysis of agent cost confirms that efficiency is task dependent and poorly addressed by static design choices [9]. In the lifelong setting specifically, LAB’s group self consistency [10] stabilizes performance under large replay buffers but at higher token cost than naïve replay, moving against the efficiency objective. LIMBO brings inference time compute control to the lifelong setting and treats memory use itself as a controllable action.

Replay Representation and Selection. Recent work has explored replay from several perspectives, including prompt compression, memory selection, and structured memory representations. LongLLMLingua [4, 11] compresses prompts to reduce token usage, but replay trajectories are sequential action demonstrations rather than static documents, making compression alone insufficient. Isele and Cosgun [12] proposed principled replay selection criteria, while SuRe [13] prioritizes replay using surprise scores computed from dual LoRA adapters, requiring access to model weights and limiting applicability to black-box LLMs. MemRL [14], ATLAS [15], CER [20], and JitRL [21] improve memory representation or retrieval, but do not explicitly optimize the inference-time cost of replay under a unified lifelong learning framework. In contrast, LIMBO formulates replay as a cost-aware inference-time decision problem, selecting replay actions on a per-sample basis to balance performance and computational cost.

III LIMBO Framework

III-A Overview

Figure 2 presents our LIMBO instantiation of lifelong inference allocation, which includes: (i) a stream of interactive tasks, (ii) a memory bank of successful interaction trajectories, (iii) online feature extraction from the current prompt, the retrieval state, and recent runtime statistics, (iv) a two head contextual bandit that predicts correctness and cost for each candidate action, and (v) prompt construction and agent execution under the selected replay mode and compute budget. After each task completes, the observed outcome and measured cost update both the memory bank and the bandit statistics.

LIMBO turns replay from a fixed preprocessing step into an online compute allocation decision. The memory bank stores only completed trajectories with measured outcomes and cost. For a new task, the controller compares memory modes and compute budgets using features that are available before the agent acts. The chosen action determines how much history enters the prompt and how much execution budget the agent receives. After the agent runs once, observed correctness and cost update both the memory bank and the controller.

III-B Problem Setup

Let 𝒯=(T1,T2,…,TN)\mathcal{T}=(T_{1},T_{2},\ldots,T_{N}) be a sequential task stream. At step ii, the agent receives task TiT_{i}, executes an interactive session, and produces a final answer. After completion, the benchmark returns a binary correctness signal yi∈{0,1}y_{i}\in\{0,1\} and a measured cost ci≥0c_{i}\geq 0. We write the completed session as σi=(Ti,yi,ci,τi)\sigma_{i}=(T_{i},y_{i},c_{i},\tau_{i}), where τi\tau_{i} is the full interaction trajectory: the task prompt, the agent’s actions at each round, the environment observations and tool outputs they produced, and the final answer. The agent maintains a memory buffer of previously successful sessions,

ℳi={σj:j<i,yj=1},\mathcal{M}_{i}=\{\sigma_{j}:j<i,\;y_{j}=1\}\,,

which can be injected into the prompt for future tasks. Whether injection helps depends on relevance: a past trajectory transfers value primarily when it shares operations, schema, or action format with the current task. For example, a past DBBench session executing a JOIN with GROUP BY is informative for a new task requiring the same SQL primitives, but adds only prompt overhead for an unrelated single-table SELECT.

The measured cost cic_{i} is the total token count of the completed session (prompt plus generation) multiplied by the provider’s per-token schedule, or the standardized schedule described in Section IV-A for local backbones. Because absolute cost magnitudes vary by orders of magnitude across backbones and environments, the controller operates on a normalized cost c^i∈[0,1]\hat{c}_{i}\in[0,1]: we maintain a running maximum Cimax=maxj≤i⁡cjC^{\max}_{i}=\max_{j\leq i}c_{j} and set c^i=ci/Cimax\hat{c}_{i}=c_{i}/C^{\max}_{i}. A cost weight λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, introduced in Eq. (5), controls how strongly the controller trades accuracy against cost: λ=0\lambda{=}0 recovers pure accuracy maximization, while large λ\lambda biases selection toward the cheapest arm. We use λ=0.5\lambda{=}0.5 in all reported experiments.

Even when memory is relevant, injection comes at a cost: it lengthens the prompt, raises API spend, and can destabilize the agent’s action formatting. Our goal is therefore not merely to store memory, but to allocate it adaptively.

III-C Memory Actions

Before solving task TiT_{i}, the controller chooses an action ai∈𝒜a_{i}\in\mathcal{A} specifying both a compute budget and a memory mode:

mi∈{none,full,compressed,retrieved}.m_{i}\in\{\texttt{none},\;\texttt{full},\;\texttt{compressed},\;\texttt{retrieved}\}. (1)

No replay (none): the task is solved without injecting past trajectories.

Full replay (full): the prompt receives a fixed number of recent successful trajectories verbatim [22], corresponding to the standard replay baseline in LifelongAgentBench.

Compressed replay (compressed): past trajectories are compressed using a LongLLMLingua style question aware wrapper before injection. The current task instruction serves as the compression query and each replay trajectory is a separate context block.

Retrieved replay (retrieved): the controller retrieves the most relevant trajectories from a larger memory bank, similar in spirit to retrieval-augmented generation [23] but applied to prior interaction traces rather than external documents. In the DBBench implementation, sessions are scored by

r(σj,Ti)=wℓJac(qi,qj)+wsJac(Si,Sj)+wb 1[bi=bj]+ϵ,r(\sigma_{j},T_{i})=w_{\ell}\,\mathrm{Jac}(q_{i},q_{j})+w_{s}\,\mathrm{Jac}(S_{i},S_{j})+w_{b}\,\mathbf{1}[b_{i}{=}b_{j}]+\epsilon, (2)

where qiq_{i} is the tokenized instruction, SiS_{i} is the skill set, bib_{i} is the table identifier, and ϵ\epsilon is a recency tie breaking bonus. The weights (wℓ,ws,wb)(w_{\ell},w_{s},w_{b}) were selected through a small hyperparameter-tuning pass on a held-out development subset, separate from all reported test runs, and held fixed across all retrieval-based variants (retrieved replay, retrieval++LongLLMLingua, and failure-aware retrieval) so differences between methods are not attributable to per-method retrieval retuning. The top kk retrieved trajectories are then injected.

Trajectory rendering

Trajectories from ℳi\mathcal{M}_{i} can be injected verbatim (raw) or in a deterministic trimmed-trace rendering that compresses verbose tool outputs while preserving the agent’s action format. Trimmed traces truncate long environment responses (e.g., stdout blocks in OS Interaction or table dumps in DBBench) and collapse repeated outputs, but keep all agent-issued commands intact. This contrasts with token-level compression (e.g., LongLLMLingua), which can damage the structured action syntax that interactive environments require. Both raw and trimmed-trace rendering are evaluated as baselines in Section IV.

III-D LIMBO Controller

Before specifying the controller, we state four properties that an inference-time memory allocator for lifelong agents must satisfy. D1: Black-box compatibility. The controller cannot require model weights, gradients, or internal activations, so the same mechanism can allocate memory for both open-weight and commercial API backbones. D2: Single-pass online learning. The controller must adapt during the task stream itself, without a separate offline training phase or a warm-start dataset. D3: Bounded per-task overhead. Controller decision cost must be small compared to the LLM call it schedules; overhead that grows with the task count is not viable at 500500-task horizons. D4: Explicit cost objective. Memory injection consumes a shared inference budget with retrieval, reasoning, and tool use, so accuracy and cost must be traded as first-class objectives. The remainder of this section instantiates a controller that satisfies all four.

We frame allocation as a contextual bandit rather than full reinforcement learning both to satisfy D1 and D2 (weight-free updates driven by per-task outcomes), and because per-task action selection has no long-horizon credit assignment (the reward signal is observed before the next task arrives), and rather than supervised learning because no ground-truth optimal action is available for any task. Contextual bandits [24, 25] are the matching abstraction: they explore actions, observe outcomes, and update online from a single scalar reward signal per decision. LIMBO is a gradient-free contextual bandit for inference-time allocation, extending the LinUCB formulation [24] with a two-head parameterization for joint accuracy and cost prediction. It selects a budget primitive ai∈𝒜a_{i}\in\mathcal{A} before each task. Each primitive specifies a replay mode, token budget, maximum round count, and tool call budget. The retrieval gated action set used in our DB experiments is shown in Table I.

Compression gated experiments use analogous primitives with compressed in place of retrieved.

Feature Vector

Before each task TiT_{i}, the controller builds a feature vector 𝐱i∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} from lightweight online signals:

𝐱i=[1,p~i,u~i,s~i,f~i,ui/pi,ℓ~i,c¯i,r¯i,c^i−1, 1[yi−1=1], 1[erri−1]]⊤,\mathbf{x}_{i}=\bigl[1,\;\tilde{p}_{i},\;\tilde{u}_{i},\;\tilde{s}_{i},\;\tilde{f}_{i},\;u_{i}/p_{i},\;\tilde{\ell}_{i},\;\\ \bar{c}_{i},\;\bar{r}_{i},\;\hat{c}_{i-1},\;\mathbf{1}[y_{i-1}{=}1],\;\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{err}_{i-1}]\bigr]^{\!\top}, (3)

The 1212 features fall into three groups. Prompt-shape features (p~i,u~i,s~i,f~i,ui/pi,ℓ~i\tilde{p}_{i},\tilde{u}_{i},\tilde{s}_{i},\tilde{f}_{i},u_{i}/p_{i},\tilde{\ell}_{i}) are log-normalized token counts for the full prompt, last user turn, system prompt, and scaffold, together with the last-user share and the normalized skill count. These capture the size and composition of the incoming task, distinguishing retrieval-heavy prompts from tool-heavy ones and flagging tasks that would exceed context if replay were added. Runtime-state features (c¯i,r¯i,c^i−1\bar{c}_{i},\bar{r}_{i},\hat{c}_{i-1}) are the EMA of normalized cost, the running accuracy, and the previous sample’s normalized cost. These let the controller condition on drift, shifting allocation when recent tasks have been unusually expensive or unusually successful without waiting for per-arm statistics to converge. Previous-outcome features (𝟏[yi−1=1],𝟏[erri−1]\mathbf{1}[y_{i-1}{=}1],\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{err}_{i-1}]) are binary indicators for whether the last task succeeded and whether it terminated in an error state; recent errors typically indicate a budget or format failure the controller can respond to by increasing the compute-budget tier. All features are computed before the LLM call for task TiT_{i} and require no weight access, satisfying D1; extraction is 𝒪⁡(|Ti|)\mathcal{O}(|T_{i}|) in the prompt length, dominated by tokenization that is required anyway.

Two Head LinUCB

LIMBO maintains one precision matrix Aa∈ℝd×dA_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} per action and two parameter vectors 𝐛aacc\mathbf{b}_{a}^{\mathrm{acc}}, 𝐛acost∈ℝd\mathbf{b}_{a}^{\mathrm{cost}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:

θ^aacc\displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{a}^{\mathrm{acc}} =Aa−1​𝐛aacc,\displaystyle=A_{a}^{-1}\mathbf{b}_{a}^{\mathrm{acc}}, θ^acost\displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{a}^{\mathrm{cost}} =Aa−1​𝐛acost.\displaystyle=A_{a}^{-1}\mathbf{b}_{a}^{\mathrm{cost}}. (4)

Head 1 estimates the correctness probability, p^a​(𝐱)=σ⁡(θ^aacc⊤​𝐱)\hat{p}_{a}(\mathbf{x})=\sigma(\hat{\theta}_{a}^{\mathrm{acc}\top}\mathbf{x}), and Head 2 estimates normalized expected cost, c^a​(𝐱)=max⁡(θ^acost⊤​𝐱,0)\hat{c}_{a}(\mathbf{x})=\max(\hat{\theta}_{a}^{\mathrm{cost}\top}\mathbf{x},0).

Action Selection

Given a cost weight λ>0\lambda>0 and an exploration coefficient α>0\alpha>0, the controller selects

ai∗=arg⁡maxa∈𝒜​[p^a​(𝐱i)−λ​c^a​(𝐱i)]+α​𝐱i⊤​Aa−1​𝐱i.a_{i}^{*}=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\;\bigl[\hat{p}_{a}(\mathbf{x}_{i})-\lambda\hat{c}_{a}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\bigr]+\alpha\sqrt{\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}A_{a}^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i}}. (5)

Selection is performed before replay injection so that the chosen mode determines how the prompt is constructed, making memory use a primary decision variable rather than a fixed preprocessing step.

Online Update

After task TiT_{i} completes, the bandit state is updated:

Aai\displaystyle A_{a_{i}} ←Aai+𝐱i​𝐱i⊤,\displaystyle\leftarrow A_{a_{i}}+\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}, (6)
𝐛aiacc\displaystyle\mathbf{b}_{a_{i}}^{\mathrm{acc}} ←𝐛aiacc+yi​𝐱i,𝐛aicost←𝐛aicost+c^i​𝐱i.\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathbf{b}_{a_{i}}^{\mathrm{acc}}+y_{i}\mathbf{x}_{i},\quad\mathbf{b}_{a_{i}}^{\mathrm{cost}}\leftarrow\mathbf{b}_{a_{i}}^{\mathrm{cost}}+\hat{c}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{i}. (7)

The inverse Aai−1A_{a_{i}}^{-1} is maintained via the Sherman Morrison rank one update in 𝒪⁡(d2)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}):

Aai−1←Aai−1−(Aai−1​𝐱i)​(Aai−1​𝐱i)⊤1+𝐱i⊤​Aai−1​𝐱i.A_{a_{i}}^{-1}\leftarrow A_{a_{i}}^{-1}-\frac{(A_{a_{i}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i})(A_{a_{i}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i})^{\top}}{1+\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\top}A_{a_{i}}^{-1}\mathbf{x}_{i}}. (8)

No gradients are computed; no model weights are modified.

Complexity

Per task, LIMBO performs one Sherman–Morrison update (Eq. 8) at 𝒪⁡(d2)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}) per action and |𝒜||\mathcal{A}| dot products to score arms, for 𝒪⁡(|𝒜|​d2)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{A}|\,d^{2}) total, with d=12d=12 and |𝒜|≤12|\mathcal{A}|\leq 12 in our experiments. Controller overhead is under 0.50.5 ms per task on a single CPU core, negligible next to the seconds of LLM inference it schedules. Memory footprint per action is 𝒪⁡(d2)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}), dominated by the precision matrix AaA_{a}: 12×12×812\times 12\times 8 bytes ≈1.2\approx 1.2 KB per arm. LIMBO therefore satisfies D3 with substantial headroom, and scales linearly in |𝒜||\mathcal{A}| if the action space is later enlarged.

Full Algorithm and Online Adaptation

Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete online loop. On each task, LIMBO interleaves action selection (lines 7–12) with the post-task bandit update (lines 15–17). Since there is no separate offline training phase, the controller continuously adapts throughout deployment.

III-E Instantiation in This Work

We study LIMBO through three action space designs:

  1. 1.

    Compression gated: arms choose among no replay, full recent replay, and LongLLMLingua compressed replay.

  2. 2.

    Retrieval gated: arms choose among no replay, full recent replay, and relevance retrieved replay (top kk from a 64 session memory bank, with k∈{4,8,16}k\in\{4,8,16\} tested as separate configs).

  3. 3.

    Retrieval gated plus rescue: the retrieval gated bandit is augmented with a confidence triggered second pass that reruns low confidence samples with maximum retrieved context.

This progression separates which memories are worth keeping from when any memory is worth spending tokens on. LIMBO addresses the second question directly while remaining compatible with multiple answers to the first.

IV Experimental Analysis

IV-A Setup

Benchmark and tasks

We evaluate on LifelongAgentBench (LAB) [10] using DB (SQL) and OS (bash) environments, each with the 500-task sequential slice released with LAB. Three backbones—Qwen2.5 7B Instruct, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, and GPT-4o mini—are evaluated on both environments, yielding six (model, environment) settings. All reported LIMBO and baseline points are averaged over three matched seeds (4242, 4343, 4444); within-cell comparisons use matched seeds throughout.

Baselines

Throughout, kk denotes the number of past successful trajectories injected per task. We compare against: No replay (zero-shot per task); Fixed replay (k=Nk{=}N), the NN most recent successful trajectories injected verbatim in a deterministic trimmed-trace rendering that preserves executable action structure (this consistently beats token-level compression at matched budget, e.g., 51.5%51.5\% vs. 49.4%49.4\% on Qwen OS at k=1k{=}1); LongLLMLingua [4], question-aware token-level compression applied to the same recent-replay buffer; and Group Self-Consistency (GSC) at usc=1\text{usc}{=}1, LAB’s native voting-based stabilizer [10].

The LIMBO configuration used across cells

All six reported LIMBO points use the same controller formulation, the same feature vector (Eq. (3)), the same online update, and the same 4-way memory action space (none, full, compressed, retrieved) paired with three generation-budget tiers (low ≤512\leq 512, medium 768768, high ≥1024\geq 1024). Retrieval scoring weights in Eq. (2) are wℓ=0.35w_{\ell}{=}0.35, ws=0.50w_{s}{=}0.50, wb=0.15w_{b}{=}0.15 and are held fixed across every retrieval-based method. The memory-bank size is 6464 in every cell. The environment-specific choice is the retrieved-kk selected inside the retrieved action: DB cells expose top-88, OS cells expose top-11, matching the strongest fixed-replay setting for each environment.

Metrics and infrastructure

We report accuracy and total token cost (USD-equivalent per 500-task run). Open-weight backbones run locally through Hugging Face transformers in bfloat16 on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs; GPT-4o mini via the OpenAI API. Decoding is greedy with a 512-token per-response cap. Costs use provider API rates for GPT-4o mini and a standardized $0.04/$0.10 per million input/output tokens for local 7B/8B models; local-model dollar values are standardized proxies rather than measured serving expense.

IV-B Overall Cost–Accuracy Tradeoff

Table II and Figure 3 summarize LIMBO’s performance across all six (model, environment) settings.

Two patterns hold across all six settings. First, LIMBO lies on the empirical cost–accuracy Pareto frontier in every cell: no fixed method is simultaneously cheaper and more accurate. Second, across the six cells LIMBO matches or exceeds the strongest memory-augmented baseline’s accuracy (within −3.8-3.8 to +0.6+0.6 points) while reducing cost by 2626–83%83\%; on GPT-4o mini OS it strictly Pareto-dominates the LongLLMLingua baseline, exceeding its accuracy by 0.60.6 points at 40.5%40.5\% lower cost.

The comparison against voting-based stabilization is clean. LAB’s GSC baseline is strictly dominated by LIMBO in all four matched settings (Qwen DB, Qwen OS, Llama DB, Llama OS): higher accuracy and lower cost. On Llama DB the accuracy gap is +26+26 points at lower cost. Voting cannot recover replay value when the underlying replay is applied indiscriminately.

The largest cost reductions (∼83%\sim 83\%) occur where the strongest baseline commits to a k=16k{=}16-scale replay budget (Qwen DB and GPT-4o mini DB). In these cells the no-replay baseline is already strong, so raw accuracy differences are modest and the cost saving carries the story. The Llama DB cell tells the opposite story: no-replay performs poorly at 20.8%20.8\%, and LIMBO reaches 66.2%66.2\% (+45.4+45.4 points over no-replay, within 3.83.8 points of fixed-replay) at less than half the fixed-replay cost. This is the clearest memory-essential regime in our evaluation. On GPT-4o mini OS, LIMBO strictly Pareto-dominates the LongLLMLingua baseline (+0.6+0.6 points at 40.5%40.5\% lower cost) and lifts accuracy by +3.4+3.4 points over no-replay at essentially the same cost.

IV-C Policy Across Backbones and Environments

Figure 4 shows the memory-action mix LIMBO converges to across all six settings under the same controller, features, action space, and hyperparameters (retrieved-kk set as described in Section IV-A). The learned policy differs sharply across cells.

DB cells (Qwen, GPT-4o mini): low-replay regime

No-replay accuracy is already high (73.0%73.0\% and 66.4%66.4\% respectively) and injecting past trajectories yields only 22–33 points of accuracy at a 55–6×6\times cost multiplier. LIMBO places ≈78%\approx 78\% of tasks on no-replay paired with the lowest generation-budget tier, spending negligible additional memory or compute.

Qwen OS: moderate-replay regime

Replay meaningfully improves accuracy (+5+5 points from no-replay to fixed k=1k{=}1) but each additional trajectory adds substantial cost. LIMBO adopts a mixed policy: retrieved k=1k{=}1 on ≈70%\approx 70\% of tasks, full replay on ≈25%\approx 25\%, with the higher generation-budget tiers used more than half the time. The result matches fixed-replay accuracy at 34%34\% lower cost.

Llama DB: memory-essential regime

Llama performs poorly on DB without prior demonstrations (20.8%20.8\%). LIMBO shifts ≈85%\approx 85\% of tasks onto retrieved replay while still keeping the majority of tasks in the lowest generation-budget tier, recovering 66.2%66.2\% accuracy at less than half the strongest baseline’s cost. The controller invests in memory when the backbone requires it rather than defaulting to a cheap policy.

GPT-4o mini OS: high-per-token-cost regime

Under commercial API pricing, LIMBO selects retrieved k=1k{=}1 on ≈88%\approx 88\% of tasks and pairs it with the medium generation tier; because the retrieved arm carries a small per-task memory footprint, aggregate cost remains within ∼6%\sim 6\% of no-replay while accuracy improves by +3.4+3.4 points. We describe this as an observed operating point rather than a demonstrated causal adaptation to the pricing schedule; a direct cost-structure ablation is future work.

The unifying observation is that the optimal memory-and-compute policy is not a global constant. It depends on the backbone’s raw capability, the environment’s replay-sensitivity, and the deployment’s per-token cost, and LIMBO exposes this variation online without any per-cell tuning or offline retraining.

IV-D Online Adaptation over the Task Stream

Figure 4 shows the converged policy after the full 500-task stream but does not by itself distinguish a bandit that learns online from one that quickly settles into a fixed mixture. Figure 5 closes this gap on Qwen OS, the setting with the most mixed converged policy. Panel (a) shows that the memory-action mix in the first 50 tasks is substantially more exploratory than the converged mix: no-replay selections drop from 17.3%17.3\% to a windows-2–10 mean of 3.8%3.8\%, full replay from 34.0%34.0\% to 23.5%23.5\%, and retrieved replay rises from 48.7%48.7\% to 72.7%72.7\%. Panel (b) provides internal-state evidence for the same trajectory: the α\alpha-scaled UCB uncertainty bonus α​x⊤​Aa−1​x\alpha\sqrt{x^{\top}A_{a}^{-1}x} for the selected action decreases by 67%67\% from the first 100 tasks to the last 100 (0.347→0.1150.347\to 0.115) because the per-action precision matrices AaA_{a} accumulate observations across the single-pass stream. The decline is monotonic in eight of nine window transitions, with one small reversal at window 7 to 8 that stays within the cross-seed standard deviation. Together, the shift in selected action mix and the contraction of the associated exploration bonus provide direct evidence that the converged policy in Figure 4 is learned during the stream rather than fixed in advance.

IV-E Discussion

Across three backbones and two environments, LIMBO occupies the cost-efficient region of the Pareto frontier that fixed replay and voting-based stabilization do not reach. On Qwen OS it matches the fixed-replay baseline within 0.10.1 points at 34%34\% lower cost; on Llama DB it stays within 3.83.8 points of fixed k=16k{=}16 at 54%54\% lower cost, in a regime where no-replay collapses to 20.8%20.8\%; on Qwen DB and GPT-4o mini DB it recognizes that additional memory does not pay off and stays within 22 accuracy points of the strongest baseline at roughly one-sixth the cost; on GPT-4o mini OS it strictly Pareto-dominates the LongLLMLingua baseline (+0.6+0.6 points at 40%40\% lower cost) while improving on no-replay accuracy by +3.4+3.4 points. In every cell the learned action mix differs qualitatively across model and environment, and the same controller instantiation reaches those different mixes online without per-cell tuning or offline retraining.

DBBench plays the role of a control environment on strong backbones, where the controller’s task is largely to recognize that additional memory does not pay off and stay cheap. LIMBO does this successfully, matching the standard fixed-replay baseline at one-sixth its cost. LIMBO’s contribution across settings is therefore frontier competitiveness: recovering most of the accuracy of the strongest memory-augmented baseline while operating close to the no-replay cost floor.

LIMBO focuses on inference time memory allocation rather than memory representation. It acts as a cost aware control layer that decides when to use memory and how much compute to allocate, complementing methods that improve how memories are stored or retrieved. For example, while MemRL [14] optimizes memory retrieval utility on strong backbones, LIMBO learns whether replay is beneficial for the current task and what budget should be allocated to it. Improved memory representations can be naturally integrated as additional replay actions in LIMBO’s action space.

V Conclusion

We introduced LIMBO, the first online inference-time memory allocation framework for lifelong LLM agents. LIMBO uses a gradient-free contextual bandit to jointly select replay strategies and inference budgets without modifying the underlying agent. Across three LLM backbones on LifelongAgentBench, LIMBO achieves better cost–accuracy tradeoffs than state-of-the-art memory-augmented baselines, maintaining comparable performance while reducing inference cost by up to ∼\sim83% (∼\sim53% on average). The learned policies adapt across models and environments, demonstrating that effective memory allocation can be discovered online rather than manually specified. These results highlight a broader opportunity for cost-aware online control of inference-time resources in lifelong LLM agents.
